solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: The only soldier without a grave

indicators.note: to go without something is to lack it, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: the sole one is the only one
a man is an ordinary soldier
taken as written, and removed

explanation.surface: A lone soldier lies dead with no grave to mark him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave' reads as a burial place, but it is the adjective meaning serious; MAN loses its A to leave MN.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a serious, sober manner or expression, as in a grave or solemn face.

clue.text: Remarkable time bird is around

indicators.note: a thing that is around another surrounds it, wrapping it on both sides

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
a starling is a common songbird

explanation.surface: Someone marvels at how a bird keeps such good time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird is around' reads as a bird hanging about; it means the bird's name wraps round the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something startling is surprising enough to be worth comment, which is what remarkable conveys.

clue.text: King’s up for a drink

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: regal means belonging to or befitting a king

explanation.surface: The king is awake and ready for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King's' must be read as the adjective REGAL, not a possessive; 'up' turns it over in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Lager is a light, bottom-fermented beer, one of the commonest drinks ordered in a pub.

clue.text: Start of month: occasion for going to sea

definitions.note: a phrase standing for an adjective describing seafaring

blocks.note: the first day of March can be written Mar I, with the Roman numeral for one
an occasion is a time, as in 'the last time'

explanation.surface: A sailor notes that the first of the month is the date to set sail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start of month' tempts you to take just M, but here it is a date: Mar I, the first of March.
explanation.definitionFit: Maritime describes anything connected with the sea, shipping and seafaring voyages.

clue.text: Flounce downstairs after no end of rage

indicators.note: with no end, a word loses its final letter
one piece coming after another means it is placed second in the across entry

blocks.note: fury is violent anger, and it loses its last letter
below is a nautical and domestic word for downstairs

explanation.surface: Someone storms off in a temper and flounces down the stairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flounce' looks like a verb for stomping off in a huff; it is the noun for a dress frill.
explanation.definitionFit: A flounce is a gathered strip of fabric on a skirt; a furbelow is the same ornamental ruffle or trimming.

clue.text: View audience has in burst of sun shows displeasing quality

indicators.note: a burst scatters things apart, so the letters land in a fresh arrangement
to have one thing in another is to hold it inside

blocks.note: sightlines are the lines of view a theatre audience has of the stage
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A burst of sunshine spoils the audience's view of the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'View audience has' is a theatre term for the lines of sight from the seats; 'shows' looks like part of the picture but only joins the halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsightliness is the state of being ugly to look at, an unpleasing quality in appearance.

clue.text: Youngster holds search, not the first, for reward

indicators.note: the opening letter is the first, so it is the one dropped
to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a boy is a youngster
a hunt is a search, here losing its first letter

explanation.surface: A child joins a search party hoping to claim a reward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For reward' looks like the purpose of the search; 'for' only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A bounty is money offered as a reward, typically for capturing a wanted person or killing vermin.

clue.text: Keen to take in one nearly new feature

indicators.note: nearly all of a word means it stops just short, losing its final letter
to take something in is to absorb it inside oneself

blocks.note: to keen is to wail in grief, which is to lament
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written, then cut short

explanation.surface: Someone is eager to include a nearly new item as a selling point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' reads as eager, but it is the verb for wailing in grief over the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A lineament is a distinctive characteristic, especially a facial feature or contour of the face.

clue.text: Was sporting about loss eventually, having come off this?

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer: the answer completes the phrase 'come off ...'

indicators.note: what comes eventually comes at the end, so only the closing letter is kept
about means around, so one piece is placed round the other

blocks.note: to sport clothes is to wear them, and the past tense is wore
the final letter of loss

explanation.surface: A sore loser behaved badly after a defeat, and the question is how badly he came off.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole phrase: someone who has lost has come off WORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To come off worse is an idiom for losing a contest or getting the inferior outcome.

clue.text: Predicted month no way looking hot

indicators.note: 'no' says the following item is absent, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: August is a month of the year
St is the abbreviation for street, a way; it is removed
someone who looks hot is red in the face

explanation.surface: A forecaster predicted that the month would bring no relief from the heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way' is the usual crossword pointer to street, abbreviated; the month must be the long form to lose it.
explanation.definitionFit: To augur is to foretell or be a sign of the future, so augured is a past-tense synonym.

clue.text: Acted in unison to scupper public attacks

indicators.note: to scupper is to sink or wreck, so the letters are wrecked and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written, all thirteen letters

explanation.surface: A group joined forces to sink some public criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole three-word phrase is the fodder, which a solver may not spot because it reads so naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: Denunciations are open condemnations of someone, made in public to discredit or accuse them.

clue.text: Taser which is initially fired into one getting tanned

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept
something fired into a target ends up lodged inside it

blocks.note: the opening letter of the weapon's name
a sunner is someone sunbathing, a word in Chambers

explanation.surface: A Taser dart is fired into a sunbather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taser' does double duty: it is the definition and also supplies its own first letter. SUNNER, a rare word for a sunbather, takes the T after S.
explanation.definitionFit: A Taser is an electric weapon that disables people by shock, so it is literally a stunner.

clue.text: Pack turning towards vermin

indicators.note: turning round sends the letters back the other way

blocks.note: to means towards
a rat is a classic piece of vermin

explanation.surface: A pack of animals turns on some vermin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pack' suggests hunting dogs; it is a pack of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarot is a pack of cards used in fortune-telling, with major and minor arcana.

clue.text: Discuss terms say on new set of books I took in

indicators.note: one thing placed on another follows it in an across answer

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
eg, for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible
taken as written
to take food in is to eat it

explanation.surface: A publisher discusses the terms of taking on a new collection of books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took in' looks like absorbing or deceiving, but here it means swallowed, ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To negotiate is to bargain or confer with others in order to settle the terms of an agreement.

clue.text: Be busy skewering folly and cruelty

indicators.note: a skewer passes right through something, so one piece is run through the middle of the other

blocks.note: a place humming with activity is busy
inanity is silliness or folly

explanation.surface: A busy satirist skewers human folly and cruelty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Be busy' is a verb phrase: a hive of activity hums.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhumanity is a lack of compassion, the quality of being brutal or cruel to others.

clue.text: Marx, at a single reading initially, who aimed to finish Moby Dick

definitions.text: who aimed to finish Moby Dick
definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the person

indicators.note: initially means at the beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: Harpo was the silent one of the Marx Brothers
a single is one
the opening letter of reading

explanation.surface: Someone reads the whole of Moby Dick in a single sitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finish' looks like finishing the book, but it means killing the whale.
explanation.definitionFit: In Melville's novel the whalers' harpooners, such as Queequeg, are the crew who strike and try to kill the white whale.

clue.text: Flower shirts

blocks.note: first meaning: a river, something that flows
second meaning: T-shirts, casual short-sleeved tops

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' reads as a bloom, but in crosswords it is often 'one that flows', a river.
explanation.definitionFit: The River Tees flows into the North Sea, and tees are informal tops shaped like the letter T.

clue.text: Brat, not at home, collared by policeman informally for a fine perhaps

indicators.note: the word for at home is removed, as it is said to be absent
collared means seized round the neck, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: sarge is a casual name for a police sergeant
an urchin is a scruffy, mischievous child
to be in is to be at home; removed

explanation.surface: A truant child is caught by the local copper and perhaps fined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not at home' means the word for being at home is taken out, not that the child is absent.
explanation.definitionFit: A surcharge is an extra charge or penalty payment, and a fine is one example of such a charge.

clue.text: Weight of stupid one out of three authors?

blocks.note: dumb means stupid
the three Brontë sisters published as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell

explanation.surface: A critic weighs up which of three writers is the stupid one.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a cryptic hint: the three authors are the Brontës and their shared pen-name.
explanation.definitionFit: A dumbbell is a short bar with weights at each end, lifted in one hand for exercise.

clue.text: It’s bloody to travel by train

blocks.note: to go is to travel
RY is an abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A grumble that rail travel is a bloody nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' sounds like the British swear word for annoying, but it means literally covered in blood.
explanation.definitionFit: Gory describes something involving a lot of blood and violence, the literal sense of bloody.

clue.text: I break into office cabinet, delaying speech

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
to bust is to break
a filer is a filing cabinet in an office

explanation.surface: A burglar admits breaking into a government cabinet office, perhaps to stall a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cabinet' suggests the government's ministers; it is a piece of office furniture for papers.
explanation.definitionFit: A filibuster is a very long speech made in a legislature to delay or block a vote.

clue.text: Stalin’s colleague left to introduce uranium for energy, his final farewell?

indicators.note: one letter is brought in to take another's place, with 'for' naming the one it replaces

blocks.note: Lavrentiy Beria was Stalin's secret police chief
U is the chemical symbol for uranium
E is the symbol for energy, and is swapped out
L is short for left

explanation.surface: A Soviet colleague of Stalin is sent off, perhaps with a nuclear twist, to his end.
explanation.walkthrough: BERIA swaps its E for U, and L follows. The question mark marks the definition as a playful description.
explanation.definitionFit: A burial is the last ceremony for a dead person, so it is jokingly his final farewell to the world.

clue.text: Savoury mince of game the hotel put out

indicators.note: to put someone out is to eject them, so those letters leave

blocks.note: croquet is a lawn game played with mallets and hoops
taken as written
H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet; removed

explanation.surface: A hotel chef serves out minced game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' suggests venison or pheasant to go with mince; it is a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A croquette is a small roll of minced meat or fish, coated in breadcrumbs and fried.

clue.text: Wind timepiece up briefly that one’s broken

indicators.note: something said briefly is cut short, losing its final letter
in a down entry, going up means the letters read bottom to top
the piece is broken open to let another sit within it

blocks.note: a clock is a timepiece, here shortened
I is the Roman numeral for one; the 's is 'has'

explanation.surface: Someone winds up a clock only to find it is broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' is not the verb for a clock but the noun for gas in the gut. CLOC turns to COLC, which opens to take I.
explanation.definitionFit: Colic is painful abdominal cramping, often caused by trapped wind, especially in babies.

clue.text: Objection chapter is tough

blocks.note: a but is an objection, as in 'no ifs or buts'
ch is the abbreviation for chapter

explanation.surface: A reader complains that a chapter is hard going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tough' looks like 'difficult' for the chapter, but it means rugged and macho.
explanation.definitionFit: Butch describes someone with a strongly masculine, rugged, tough-looking appearance.

clue.text: Giant bird given a name

blocks.note: a tit is a small songbird
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A huge bird is given a name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giant bird' reads as one phrase, but 'Giant' is the definition and the bird is a tiny one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titans were the gigantic gods of Greek myth, so a titan is any person or thing of great size.

clue.text: Spots long tie being knotted

indicators.note: something knotted is twisted and tangled, so the letters are tangled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone notices a long tie with a spotted pattern being knotted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' reads as a verb for noticing; it is the noun for skin marks.
explanation.definitionFit: Lentigo is the medical term for small brown pigmented patches on the skin, like freckles.

clue.text: Industrial plant gave off stench: years, on and off

indicators.note: switching on and off by turns means every other letter is kept

blocks.note: smelt is a British past tense of smell
the second and fourth letters of years

explanation.surface: A factory has been giving off a stink, intermittently, for years.
explanation.walkthrough: SMELT is a pun too: a smelter does smelt ore, but here the word is the past tense of smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A smelter is a works where metal is extracted from ore by heating and melting it.

clue.text: Unconcerned being unable to drive round rear of village

indicators.note: the rear is the back, so only the final letter is kept
going round something encircles it

blocks.note: someone without a car cannot drive
the final letter of village

explanation.surface: A villager who cannot drive is untroubled by the ring road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being unable to drive' describes someone who owns no vehicle, an unusual but fair word.
explanation.definitionFit: Careless means not caring or worried, so it is a direct synonym for being unconcerned about something.

clue.text: Angled strike and cut on back of leg

indicators.note: the back is the end, so only the final letter is kept
one piece placed on another sits after it in an across answer

blocks.note: the final letter of leg
to lance is to cut open, as with a boil

explanation.surface: A batsman plays an angled stroke and is hit on the back of the leg.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a glance is a deflected shot off the bat's face, and leg is the side of the field behind the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A glance is a blow that strikes at an angle and slides off, rather than hitting squarely.
